titleStmt.title: Interview with Arthur J. Locke, February 19, 2003

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Arthur J. Locke was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: In an effort to preserve stories of their service by veterans of the United States military, on this 19th day of February in the year 2003, for the Veterans History Project, the information documented on this tape and enclosed transcript have been graciously offered by Arthur J. Locke who resides in the city of Hooksett, in the state of New Hampshire. This interview is being conducted at the Veterans Hospital in Manchester, New Hampshire. Mr. Locke was born on August 3, in the year 1915 and Mr. Locke served during World War II and in the Korean Wars. He served the military from 1934 to 1961 and he achieved the rank of 1st Sergeant. Mr. Lock served in the Philippines, Japan, and Germany, among other places. I, Judith Cherbonneau and volunteering in conjunction with the Veterans Hospital in Manchester, New Hampshire and am conducting and taping this interview for the project. Upon completion of this interview and documentation, this information will be sent and preserved in the Library of Congress in the Folklife Center.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Mr. Locke, were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: And where were you living at that time?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Hooksett (New Hampshire)

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: And why did you join the military? Why did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I used to read the National Geographic and I wanted to see some of these countries, which I did.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: And what were your feelings about enlisting?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: My feelings about enlisting? I thought that was a good way to travel.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: What branch did you select?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I was in the Infantry.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: In the Army?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Where you happy with that choice?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Would you tell me some of your experiences in Basic Training?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, when I joined they didn't have any Basic Training. I was in Fort Devens with whatever recruits they had. There weren't very many. Some old World War II Corporal would come out and march you around. That's all the basic training I got.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: How long were you at Fort Devens? How long did they have for any kind of training?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Their training was ...two, three weeks, that's all.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So you didn't receive any specialized training, then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: No, not really any. In 1934, the whole Army was only ninety thousand and there wasn't any such thing as Basic Training except in the regiment, when you were in there. Teach you how to drill. That's all they did. 4 Experiences

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: In what wars did you serve?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: World War II and the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Can you tell me where you were stationed? In some of the places you were stationed?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: There was Fort Devens, and then I reenlisted for the Phillippines; I was in the Phillippines and before that I went to China. I was in China. I reenlisted the first time for China. I just got there and the whole outfit left on the next boat back to the states again.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Why was that?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Because the Japanese had taken the place over. The time they sank The Penni. It was that time. So, I came back to Fort Devens and then in 1939 if you had a high- school education you could take a short discharge and reenlist in the Air Corps. So, I think there was four of us in the company, who had a highschool education. There happened to be three Italian kids and I. They wanted to go to Long Island and I said, "No, let's go to the Phillippines because I had stopped there before and had a good time, so we all went to the Phillippines. And after the war, I came back and I was stationed in radar stations all over the country and you name it...I was there; Massachusetts, North Carolina, California, Florida, Montana; I retired from Montana. I've been everywhere.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: That's interesting. So, that was...you were working radar, for the military?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Radar stations, yeah.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, how were you transported to China? Did you fly or... 5

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: We went on a transport. We got on a transport in Brooklyn and went through the Canal...San Francisco and across. That way.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: A long trip.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah, I went that way, twice, too!

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: How long did it take you to get there?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh, oh, about...at least six weeks. It took a long time.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, after your radar experiences, then where did you go?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: After your...working the radar stations where did you go after that?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: When I retired?

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: No, where did you go after...well, in between China and you said you were in Germany and...

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh, in between China I went to the Phillippines.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: How long were you there?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I was there three years and I was in Japan for three years. I was a POW.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Could you tell me about that, if it isn't too painful.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, everybody who was in the Phillippines was captured and we all went to camps in the Phillippines and they were pretty bad. After the 'Death March'...I made the 'Death March' and I wanted to get out of the Phillippines because of the malaria and it was real bad there. They had you working on building bridges and making air fields. I happened to be in Bilibid Prison where they...where they sent you when you were sick. I had malaria pretty bad, so they sent me to Bilibid Prison and I got over the malaria and I was about to be sent out in the field and they had a....was thirty five prisoners come up from the 6 islands, down south, Iloilo and Panya. There was thirty officers and five men and they wanted fifteen volunteers. I don't know how they come up with that figure, but they wanted fifteen volunteers, so I jumped right out. I was one of the volunteers. I knew if I went to Japan, it would be cool and anyhow, I wanted to see Japan. It was kind of a silly, silly thing. The Philippines was terrible. You didn't want to stay there.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, at this time you were going to go to Japan, you were still a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh yeah. Yeah. So, I went up there in October of '42. There was fifty of us on this ship. We had a very pleasant trip. We had plenty of food. We stayed on the... above deck. The only ship I ever heard of they let you stay above deck. And fifty people weren't many anyway. The ones that came after, they got sunk and bombed and I think it was five thousand POW's drowned and they come up later, you know.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: They were going to Japan?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: The ones who went early.they didn't have it so bad and I thought that, too. I said, if I waited another two years, or whatever, they are going to sinking these ships. In fact, they sank one ship out of our convoy and that was in '42. So, when we got to Colby, they let us off and marched us up the street to a brick warehouse and they got in there and there was a whole bunch of people in there, dressed up in corduroy, corduroy outfits. They were all laying down and we didn't know what happened and they wouldn't let us talk to anybody for two or three days and it turned out they were British people. British troops from Hong Kong and they had been sunk on the way over. And I don't know how many they lost. They lost a third of a ship because the bottom...the rear end of the ship went down and the front stayed up and they wouldn't let them out of the hull. They finally got out of the hull and swam about eight miles to an island. Then they took them to 7 Shanghai. Of course they didn't have any clothes and when they got to Colby...they were... I think a hundred died of pneumonia the first winter. It was a pretty bad winter and they come up from the tropics to Japan. We finally got to talk to them. There was three...about four hundred of them and then... of course we couldn't understand them unless they came from London. London, Middlesex Regiment and the Royal Scotts and they couldn't understand those people either. But, we got along good with everybody, anyway. We were only in there...then they moved all the officers out and that left just twenty, twenty Americans in this camp and we were there for the rest of the war. And next year, there were a hundred and...a hundred and fifty, two hundred Australians come in, so we got to know them pretty well. They were good people. We worked on the docks for the rest of the war. It was the best camp in Japan, bar none. I've heard stories of coal mines and steel mills and we...we ate pretty good. We were on the docks and stole everything we could think of. I worked on the rail road quite a bit and unloading cars and things all over the place. We'd go up the street...up the railroad line and there was all kinds of little gardens. Everybody over there had little garden, over there and they hated to see us come. We'd clean it out! When nobody was there, we'd just clean it out. It was no wonder they didn't kill us, but we got along pretty good. It was the best camp in Japan. I was there the whole war. I can't think it was...it was cold. I mean it was cold in the wintertime as soon as you left, in the morning, they'd open the windows and when you come in at night it was...it was a cold wind up there.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: What kind of accommodations did you have? Where did you stay? What was it like?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, they had benches...platforms. JC; Like a barracks? Or a barn? A building of some sort? 8

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: It wasn't bad. It was a brick building. A warehouse an English company had and most of the barracks up there...most of the people I ever talked to just had wooden places and they were freezing all the time, but that brick build was pretty solid and after a while six hundred people...the heat...there was a little heat. It wasn't bad at all. We had a big platform and you had about this, about this much space (demonstrates a few inches between each platform with his hands) and we had about four blankets. Of course the first winter three of us slept together, so we had eight blankets on top and four underneath.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Did you form any friendships? Really close friendships there?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh, yes. I, I still liked the people in England. Of course they are dying, now. I write to people in Australia. In fact, I've been....I went to England when I was in Germany. I took a trip up to Scotland to see some of my friends.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: When was this?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: In the fifties. Fifty one...fifty two and three and four. I was over in Germany three years. I went up there a couple times.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Do you think that helped you through your experiences in prison camp, the closeness you formed with these men? You all had something in common, obviously. Al: Well, the fact is it was run by the British. It was a British camp and they kept their discipline. They saluted. They saluted the 1st Sergeant and they ran the camp as a camp should be. American...I hate to tell you this, but the American camps were awful. The officers were awful. Once in a while, you'd get a good officer, but most of the time...you know an officer, over there, we'd have to get between the Japanese and whoever they were hitting or whatever. Now, the British did and the Australians did. They probably got 9 wacked three, four times, too, but they saved a lot of people.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, how did the British come to be managing these prison camps?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, they were there first and...I don't know how we got there or why they put us in with the British. There was only thirty of us and the thirty officers were shipped out, so that left just twenty enlisted men. We were kind of orphans. They put us in the corner., in the peak of the roof. That was nice. Up in... it was the fourth floor. There was a big space and they built a platform up in the peak of the roof, so they put us up in there, plus that was the warmest place in the place. When you had to go to the toilet, though, you had to go down four flights...four flights and on that diet you had to go every, you know, every couple hours. Rice diet. It was a pretty good camp. After hearing some of these other places, I'm glad I was in a British camp.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: How long were you...you said three years? Three and a half years?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: It was from November...October '42 until the war ended.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, how long...?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: There was...let's see...October '42...just about three years...almost.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, how did they come to tell you, you were going to be going home? That the war was over?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, there was a lot of bombing in June. In June of '45 our camp got bombed and burned out so we moved up into the mountains for...it was pretty good because nobody got killed in that bombing. There was firebombs went through the roof. Everybody had a different idea. I figured I'd be up, safer up on the top because if they dropped bombs, those bombs would go through and explode down in the bottom so I ran...half of them ran to the top and half they was afraid that... they dropped in some areas, so they ran to 10 the bottom, so like a big anthill we...was up on the top floor looking out the window and there was...you could see the roof of the other building, next to us, and all of a sudden that roof disappeared. I says, "Oh boy. "And then they come through our roof and those in incendiary areas were about six feet long and about this wide (demonstrates width with arms held apart) and like a big Roman candle they come through the roof and stick up in the floor. They were all like a birthday cake and flames all over the place. So I had my shopping bag... was all I had to put my stuff in. They stored...you know those woven store things...they have in the Phillippines? That's all I had. I took that and went downstairs. They took us out in the...there was a park outside and they took us out in this park and there was anti-aircraft out there. Japanese anti-aircraft...nobody around. There were all these holes and trenches, so we all got in the holes and after the place was burned, they marched us about seven miles up in the mountains to a camp that had...that was empty. It used to be Australians that worked in a shipyard, up there. It was nice. They had a fishpond...whatever. Nice barracks except there was fleas. You couldn't sleep. There were so many black...so many fleas zipping around all over. We were there about three weeks and I guess they decided there was too much bother to take us down to work in a truck, so they moved us down to a...still in Colby, but it was a schoolhouse we moved into. The top floor had been burned, but there was still a couple...they put us in there and that's where I was at the end of the war. We didn't have any..they burned...they burned Colby up in two...Colby's a big city and they burned it up in two raids. In fact, they burned all the big cities up. There was just nothing.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, this was the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah. 11

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Where you in the prison camp during Pearl Harbor? Did you hear anything about Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh, yeah. I was in Clarke Field, when they...in the Philippines when we heard about Pearl Harbor and I was in a new squadron and I made 1st Sergeant and they moved most of the people down in Manila because they were made up of people from every...you know, pick up ten people from each squadron to make a new outfit. They were all gone except the supply sergeant and me. We were doing up the paper work and they were going down there to join them. I woke up... it had to be a Sunday, they were there and I woke up, heard on the radio that Pearl Harbor had been bombed. I said, "Boy!" We didn't have any idea what was going to happen. I said, "I better get out of here and get back to the squadron." So I went down to the headquarters building, which was right on the flight line, at Clarke Field.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, Clarke Field is in where?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: It is in the Philippines, about sixty miles north of Manila. That is where all the bombers were. The bombers had taken off and they were flying around, somehow, just because they...it was war time, you know. So I went down to headquarters and I was right in the middle of the flight line. Nobody there; I couldn't figure out why not and I was looking out the window and there was four pursuit planes taking off and they had an old seaplane, they called the Duck, and that thing was taking off and all of a sudden all these bombs start dropping. I was looking out the window and that disappeared and two of the planes...I couldn't explain. There were forty bombers up above dropping all their bombs and there I was up on the second floor. I would have rather have been in a ditch. I didn't get hurt and then I got down and got in a, in a trench, and they come down with these fire 12 fight and strafed everything and shot everything up and all the bombers, the bombers were, the big bombers were on the ground and they all got destroyed. So I got out of there and then I got a ride in a truck down to Manila and joined my outfit down there.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: What was your duties... what was your job in the service? What did you do?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I was a 1st Sergeant, at that time. It was a brand new squadron. If it had been peacetime, it would have been a wonderful job. Headquarters of all the Far East Air Service Command, we'd have been flying all over the Far East, you know. Never got off the ground. We didn't do a thing until we got, in fact we didn't do anything for the rest of the war. They sent us over to Bataan, we drug trenches, went out a couple times. We were in a couple battles, that's about all we did. There wasn't much you could do. Nothing was coming in. They made those...we used to listen to the radio. (It broadcast) 'The biggest fleet in the history...in...was heading for the Philhppines.' That was a lot of baloney...they were headed for Australia, Nothing ever came to the Phillippines.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Why were they going to Australia?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, because they didn't dare come to the Phillippines. They would have got sunk. A couple of submarines came, but that was about it.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So you think they just., a rumor to make the enemy think they were..

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: That was a...Roosevelt didn't like MacArthur to start with and he wasn't about to... him and the Chief of Staff had been under Eisenhower had been under MacArthur in the Phillippines and MacArthur called him, "The best clerk he ever had"; which probably he was. He never forgot it and he wouldn't send a thing over to the Phillippines. He was in charge of sending things to the Phillippines...never sent a thing.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Politics. 13

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Nothing, except a couple submarines. They came to pick up nurses and officers and stuff like that.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, after the war was over and you were released, where did you go then?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: After the war, I came back, I came back to...when the war was over they came to get us. It was about a month before they came to Colby to pick us up and in the meantime, they dropped all this food and me, I always had a sweet tooth, so they had Hershey Bars and Hershey Bars and fruit salad and I stuffed myself with that and of course you know what happened. I got dysentery or almost the same thing and when they come down and picked us up and said, "How do you feel?" I said, "I feel pretty good." I told them what happened and they gave me a red, I guess it was a red tag or something. The rest of the guys got yellow tags or green tags. I got a red tag. I didn't think...so they segregated us on the, on the train. It took us a long time; we were down below; a couple hundred miles from Tokyo. There they sent us up to Tokyo, not Tokyo, but where the big... Yokohama, that's where it was; where all the fleet was and all that. They took us off the train and there were two or three of us that had red tags so they took us, put us on a hospital ship, which was nice. You got all the ice cream you wanted and lay in bed. No trouble. We were there about three days and they flew us out. They flew us...put us in a hospital plane. You can lay in bed all the way across the Pacific. The rest of the guys who didn't have the red tags... all the rest of the whole camp, they put them on planes and took them to Okinawa. And then they stayed there a bit and they flew them on...they flew them down to the Philippines and they flew from the Philippines...they put them on a ship in the Phillippines, so I was far ahead, you know, I was...I never saw any of them again, hardly. My best friend, who I 'buddied' around with in prison camp was named Rigdon 14 and he was going to get married when he got home. Come from Louisiana. We were going to Louisiana together and then he was coming up to New Hampshire. So when he got to Okinawa, they kept him there two, three days and they started flying them out to the Philippines. He got on a plane and first thing the plane did was head down into the ground. Killed him dead! Him and the whole plane load. Of course I didn't know that until I got home. Turned out his ex-girlfriend wrote me and his mother wrote me. She had already gotten married to someone else . That would have killed poor Rigdon anyway. After all the mess, he got killed on the way home!

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Do you know what happened? Why it crashed? Do you know why it crashed?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: It hardly got off the ground. If it hadn't been...if I hadn't gotten my red tag, I probably would have been with him. There were a lot of things, in that war, that I got awful lucky. I got lucky...most of the people in the Philippines didn't want to go to Japan. They thought that the United States was right around the corner and they'd be delivered in a month or two. That didn't happen, you know that. I waited three years and a half. I says, I don't think they are going to come over here that fast. I rather go to a better climate than this. It was the best move I ever made. It was the best camp in Japan. It was good trip up. No trouble. I got back, I went to California, San Francisco. Stayed there; they gave us uniforms partial payment; we visited San Francisco. We couldn't spend anything. Everybody would buy you, buy you drinks and buy you this and buy you that. We had a great time.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Take advantage of it.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Put us on, put us on the train and we got back to Fort Devens...where did they put me, but in the same, the same room I was in during peacetime; 1934. Same place! It was 15 a recuperation hospital I didn't do anything, there, at all. They just asked you how you feel. You can go home, if you want to, and come back Saturday night and they'd check on you Sunday and we'd leave Monday morning and go home again. We did that for...until I reenlisted and I got then I got three months, three months leave at home. From then on I just bounced around. I was with a radar squadron.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, when did you go to Korea?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I didn't go to Korea. I was in Germany during the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Oh, I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: We used to watch it on the news reels.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, how long were you in Germany?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Three years.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, what time was that? Was that after the war?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: That was in '52 to '55.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: We got the..well, I got a lot of medals. I don't know if I can think of them all.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Could you name just a couple?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I got the Asiatic Pacific Campaign Bar, the Good Conduct Medal, and the Bronze Star for Meritorious Conduct, over in the Phillippines. Long service medals. I had the three battle stars. All kinds of a...you get a medal about every year, like in the service. They call them medals.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, you said you were, ah, injured, but not during combat?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, not by combat, but I suppose it was a result of combat. I am one hundred percent disabled. I had Bari-Bari That's, that's as bad as being shot..worse, worse than 16 being shot, I think.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: That was while you were in the prison camp?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Ah-ah. That's because of, lack of Vitamin B-2. Of course, in the Phillippines, they gave you...we had rice, watery rice for breakfast. That is about all you had so you put sugar, you put, put sugar on it. But I see these guys with big legs...my legs swelled up. Up to my knees. You try to run, you can't run. You'd fall down. And that's an oriental disease and nobody... we never had it... Americans didn't have it because they... of their diet and when you're on a rice diet...the Filipinos don't like, don't like brown rice. They like white rice, like everybody else over there...what they do with the husks they stew up the husks and make a medicine they call Tiki-Tiki. They take a spoonful of that every morning and what that is, is Vitamin B-l. Of course, we didn't know anything about that. We never got any Tiki-Tiki. We got Bari-Bari instead. And I was looking at a medical book one of the guys had and the had something about Bari-Bari and it said something about swelling and goes up and up and when it reaches your heart, you're a dead man. Of course it was coming up my legs and I could think of that... two or three of these guys are dying. They were all swollen up. So I laid off the sugar. I didn't realize what it was doing to me, but when I got to Japan, we used to work on sugar. Nice brown sugar and we'd be eating that brown sugar and I began feeling funny put there and I went to the medic, it was a British medic and he said, "Was I eating sugar?" And I said, "Yes, of course. Everybody does." He said, "Forget the sugar. Do not eat sugar." So I didn't, from then on, but I still had Bari-Bari. It kills the nerves in your legs. You go to jump and you can't jump. It's funny. You think you're jumping, but you can't, you can't do it. But the Americans had no idea about Bari-Bari. I should have been retired on disability, but even 17 when I got my...when I retired and took my physical, I told them about it and they didn't know anything about it. And when I got back here and retired and come to the, come to the VA here, they had a Filipino woman and she was giving me Thiamin. You could smell me all over the place. Thiamin you can smell that stuff. It was too late, then. I was done and my legs were all gone and when they wanted to...they took me down to Boston for...they wanted to study me for Bari-Bari and that.what it does, it delays the reaction...the nerves...the sheaths...the nerves are gone and whatever message is getting down there, if I tell my foot to do this, there is a delay, there. They stuck a wire up here and another wire down there and they were giving me jolts of electricity to see the reaction time. That's how I got one hundred percent disability because they would give me a shock and it would be a while, but my leg would jump. And besides that, you know, when they tap your knee here and your leg jumps, I have no reaction at all. I've had guys and they take a physical, you know, they, the doctor, (says) "Put your leg..." taps me and expects it, expects something to happen and nothing happens. He taps, tap, tap, tap, tap, tap, says, "How come?" And finally, I have to tell him, "Bari-Bari, there's no reaction." So, that's how I got one hundred percent; amongst other things.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: How do you think your service effected you, mentally or did it bother you?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: It didn't effect me at all, mentally. I know it effects some people. They go into a shell and will not talk about it. They have bad dreams and you know, all that. I have had bad dreams, but I dreamed I was a POW, but it was never as bad as it really was. Something like going back and visiting, you know? I never had, what you could call; I never woke up in a sweat or anything like that. I just think it's a...I don't know whether it's your mental capacity or not, you know. I was always, what you could call, pretty 18 smart. I keep my brain going. I read a lot and do all kinds of puzzles all the time. A lot of guys don't do anything except have a beer and, you know, I think them are the kind of people that it effects.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Hum, they might not have had your willpower?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Must be something.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now is a good time, I am going to turn the tape. End Of Side A Of Arthur J. Locke Interview 19 After Service

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: I have turned the tape over and I am continuing the interview with Arthur J. Locke of Hooksett,New Hampshire.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Mr. Locke, do you recall the day your service ended? When you retired.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh yes.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Where were you stationed on your last days?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I was stationed in Cut Bank, Montana.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Now, did you come right home, ah, to Hooksett after that?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah, I came right home. I expected..I always thought when I retired, I would have a review. But, I was up in the radar station....I was one hundred and fifty miles from an Air Force base. I heard nothing about the review. I was pretty mad anyhow because I didn't want to retire, but I had...they come up with a order that said if you had ten years commission time and twenty years enlisted time..no, you couldn't do a thing about it. You retired. I didn't want to get out. I wanted to do my thirty years. And I was pretty mad, anyway. You know, I didn't even get invited to a review. I was t'd off.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: I imagine.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I got in my car and drove off all the way across... I went up into Canada and come across.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Did you feel that the time you had spent...they weren't grateful for your service? 20 Were you kind of upset that you don't feel they were appreciative of your service?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: No, I don't! It's just like they kick you out the door. 21 Later Years and Closing

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: When you came home did you go to work or go to school?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I went to work. I went to work and went to school at the same time. I went to night school and day school and correspondence school and I got a...I got an Associate Degree and when I had that I had enough credits...I had about a hundred credits at that time. I always used to take correspondence courses, whether...I had to take specific courses.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: What courses could those be?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Ah, they were all different, different branches of whatever... and ah, we had to have... you had to have different ones to graduate. So many points in this, so of course I had to keep on going. When I got done, I had all kinds of points. I had... I got my degree in General, Bachelor of General Studies. Specializing in oriental study. In fact, I took a class at Mount Saint Mary's in Hooksett, the last year they operated up there. You know, Mount Saint Mary's?

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: It was the last year and it was the only place I could get any Chinese history. Okay, I was the only man who went to school at Mount Saint Mary's and this was the last credits that I needed and that was the only place I could get it, around here. I taught the class because I was in China! I had a pretty good time up there. They were all girls. They closed the place up and when I got my degree, I had to give a speech because I was the 22 Valedictorian of the class over to the branch...Merrimack Valley branch, over there. I had to make a speech.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Did you use the, V. I., the V.I...the G.I. Bill?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah, it never cost me anything. I had enough years, I could have gone to school for the rest of my life.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: And taught all the classes.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Did you join any veterans organizations or are you a member of any now?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Oh yeah. I joined the Legion. I just became a member of the Disabled American Veterans. They had.I joined the V.F.W. They had a..they had one in Hooksett and when it faded out I just never...I should belong to that, but I don't. I belong to the Veterans of Bataan and Corregidor and American Ex-POW's. Quite a few, different ones.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Did your military service influence your thinking about war or military service in general?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I suppose it did. You find a lot of mistakes people made and things they should have did, they didn't. Right now, I think, you can't let things build up. You have to cut them off before they start. That's my idea, anyway.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: You are referring to the present situation?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah. All these people are demonstrating against this and that and they don't know what they're doing because they never had the experience that I had. I could see the experience of being unprepared. Of which, we were unprepared.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: In referring to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: How do you feel about the United States and the military today? 23

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I have a grandson in the Army. He did three years walking 'post' in Washington on the Unknown Soldier. Now he's in Germany. I guess he's in Germany. He went on...to the Middle East, too. I don't know. They..sometimes, I think they're doing alright and then, I don't know.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Do you feel today's citizens are patriotic?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, we were all patriotic after the thing happened in New York, but it didn't take long for them to get back in the old...the old ways again. They forget awful quick.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: What would you do or say to influence, to influence today's youth, the younger generation about patriotism? What would you tell them?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Well, the young, the young people aren't like they used to be. I don't think they think the same way we used to. They are too busy watching television and nothing much you can say to them, I don't believe.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Do you feel every person should serve in the military, in some capacity?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I do. I think as soon as they are eighteen they should go in for three years. Bar nobody. Everybody.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Do you attend any reunions?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Not very often. I used to go to the, the ah, (American) Defenders of Bataan and Corregidor, but most of the ones I go...are the ones that...at lot of them when I got over there, the majority...just before the war started and they were only there a week or two before the war started and all the old ones that were there when I...from '39, along there, most of them are gone, so I never see anybody I know. So I quit.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we haven't covered, in this interview?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Not really, I don't think so. 24

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Any words of advice for the military today or the President, let's say?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Shoot first! That's what I say. You know, they're so worried about civilians. They should see what they did in Japan. They flattened cities of the...millions of people. They didn't care what happened to those civilians, did they? Why are they worried about it now? This isn't, this isn't the days of chivalry. They would kill us in a minute. You think the Arabs, they blow up, they blow up everybody; kids, women.

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: So, do you think we are going to be too soft again? And you think we have forgotten already?

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: Yeah. They didn't care who was in that building when they ran into it. Why should we worry about it?

sp.speaker: Judith Cherbonneau
sp.p: Well, Mr. Locke thank you for sharing your recollections with me and a bit of your life and I will see that this tape and transcript are sent to the Library of Congress for preservation. Thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Arthur Locke
sp.p: I hope they pay attention to it; which I doubt.
